# Path Parameters { #path-parameters }

## Recap { #recap }



With **FastAPI**, by using short, intuitive and standard Python type declarations, you get:

* Editor support: error checks, autocompletion, etc.
* Data "<dfn title="converting the string that comes from an HTTP request into Python data">parsing</dfn>"
* Data validation
* API annotation and automatic documentation

And you only have to declare them once.

That's probably the main visible advantage of **FastAPI** compared to alternative frameworks (apart from the raw performance).

# Path Operation Configuration { #path-operation-configuration } ## Tags { #tags } You can add tags to your *path operation*, pass the parameter `tags` with a `list` of `str` (commonly just one `str`): ```python from fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() class Item(BaseModel): name: str description: str | None = None price: float tax: float | None = None tags: set[str] = set() @app.post("/items/", tags=["items"]) async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item: return item @app.get("/items/", tags=["items"]) async def read_items(): return [{"name": "Foo", "price": 42}] @app.get("/users/", tags=["users"]) async def read_users(): return [{"username": "johndoe"}] ``` They will be added to the OpenAPI schema and used by the automatic documentation interfaces:

# First Steps { #first-steps } ## Recap, step by step { #recap-step-by-step } ### Step 3: create a *path operation* { #step-3-create-a-path-operation } #### Path { #path } "Path" here refers to the last part of the URL starting from the first `/`. So, in a URL like: ``` https://example.com/items/foo ``` ...the path would be: ``` /items/foo ``` /// note A "path" is also commonly called an "endpoint" or a "route". /// While building an API, the "path" is the main way to separate "concerns" and "resources". #### Operation { #operation } "Operation" here refers to one of the HTTP "methods". One of: * `POST` * `GET` * `PUT` * `DELETE` ...and the more exotic ones: * `OPTIONS` * `HEAD` * `PATCH` * `TRACE` In the HTTP protocol, you can communicate to each path using one (or more) of these "methods". --- When building APIs, you normally use these specific HTTP methods to perform a specific action. Normally you use: * `POST`: to create data. * `GET`: to read data. * `PUT`: to update data. * `DELETE`: to delete data. So, in OpenAPI, each of the HTTP methods is called an "operation". We are going to call them "**operations**" too. #### Define a *path operation decorator* { #define-a-path-operation-decorator } ```python from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() @app.get("/") async def root(): return {"message": "Hello World"} ``` The `@app.get("/")` tells **FastAPI** that the function right below is in charge of handling requests that go to: * the path `/` * using a get operation /// note | `@decorator` Info That `@something` syntax in Python is called a "decorator". You put it on top of a function. Like a pretty decorative hat (I guess that's where the term came from). A "decorator" takes the function below and does something with it. In our case, this decorator tells **FastAPI** that the function below corresponds to the **path** `/` with an **operation** `get`. It is the "**path operation decorator**". /// You can also use the other operations: * `@app.post()` * `@app.put()` * `@app.delete()` And the more exotic ones:

# Features { #features }

**FastAPI** gives you the following:

# Request Body { #request-body }

## Results { #results }



With just that Python type declaration, **FastAPI** will:

* Read the body of the request as JSON.
* Convert the corresponding types (if needed).
* Validate the data.
    * If the data is invalid, it will return a nice and clear error, indicating exactly where and what was the incorrect data.
* Give you the received data in the parameter `item`.
    * As you declared it in the function to be of type `Item`, you will also have all the editor support (completion, etc) for all of the attributes and their types.
* Generate [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org) definitions for your model, you can also use them anywhere else you like if it makes sense for your project.
* Those schemas will be part of the generated OpenAPI schema, and used by the automatic documentation <abbr title="User Interfaces">UIs</abbr>.

# Strict Content-Type Checking { #strict-content-type-checking }



By default, **FastAPI** uses strict `Content-Type` header checking for JSON request bodies, this means that JSON requests **must** include a valid `Content-Type` header (e.g. `application/json`) in order for the body to be parsed as JSON.

# Body - Nested Models { #body-nested-models }



With **FastAPI**, you can define, validate, document, and use arbitrarily deeply nested models (thanks to Pydantic).

# FastAPI { #fastapi }

* **Easy**: Designed to be easy to use and learn. Less time reading docs.

* **Short**: Minimize code duplication. Multiple features from each parameter declaration. Fewer bugs.

* **Robust**: Get production-ready code. With automatic interactive documentation.

* **Standards-based**: Based on (and fully compatible with) the open standards for APIs: [OpenAPI](https://github.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification) (previously known as Swagger) and [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/).

<small>* estimation based on tests conducted by an internal development team, building production applications.</small>

# Extra Data Types { #extra-data-types }

## Other data types { #other-data-types }



Here are some of the additional data types you can use:

* `UUID`:
    * A standard "Universally Unique Identifier", common as an ID in many databases and systems.
    * In requests and responses will be represented as a `str`.
* `datetime.datetime`:
    * A Python `datetime.datetime`.
    * In requests and responses will be represented as a `str` in ISO 8601 format, like: `2008-09-15T15:53:00+05:00`.
* `datetime.date`:
    * Python `datetime.date`.
    * In requests and responses will be represented as a `str` in ISO 8601 format, like: `2008-09-15`.
* `datetime.time`:
    * A Python `datetime.time`.
    * In requests and responses will be represented as a `str` in ISO 8601 format, like: `14:23:55.003`.
* `datetime.timedelta`:
    * A Python `datetime.timedelta`.
    * In requests and responses will be represented as a `float` of total seconds.
    * Pydantic also allows representing it as an "ISO 8601 time diff encoding", [see the docs for more info](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/serialization/#custom-serializers).
* `frozenset`:
    * In requests and responses, treated the same as a `set`:
        * In requests, a list will be read, eliminating duplicates and converting it to a `set`.
        * In responses, the `set` will be converted to a `list`.
        * The generated schema will specify that the `set` values are unique (using JSON Schema's `uniqueItems`).
* `bytes`:
    * Standard Python `bytes`.
    * In requests and responses will be treated as `str`.
    * The generated schema will specify that it's a `str` with `binary` "format".
* `Decimal`:
    * Standard Python `Decimal`.
    * In requests and responses, handled the same as a `float`.
* You can check all the valid Pydantic data types here: [Pydantic data types](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/usage/types/types/).

## Enhancing Path Operation Metadata & Validating/Documenting the Request Body in FastAPI

FastAPI gives you rich tools to enrich your API's documentation and ensure your request bodies are properly validated and described. Here's a complete breakdown:

---

## 🏷️ Part 1: Enhancing Path Operation Metadata

### 1. Global API Metadata

You can set top-level metadata on the `FastAPI()` app instance itself:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

description = """
ChimichangApp API helps you do awesome stuff. 🚀

## Items
You can **read items**.
"""

app = FastAPI(
    title="ChimichangApp",
    description=description,
    summary="Deadpool's favorite app. Nuff said.",
    version="0.0.1",
    terms_of_service="http://example.com/terms/",
    contact={
        "name": "Deadpoolio the Amazing",
        "url": "http://x-force.example.com/contact/",
        "email": "dp@x-force.example.com",
    },
    license_info={
        "name": "Apache 2.0",
        "url": "https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html",
    },
)
```

You can write Markdown in the `description` field and it will be rendered in the output. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/metadata/]

The available global metadata fields include `title`, `summary`, `description`, `version`, `terms_of_service`, `contact`, and `license_info`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/metadata/]

---

### 2. Tags — Grouping Path Operations

You can add `tags` to your path operations to group them in the docs: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

```python
@app.post("/items/", tags=["items"])
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    return item

@app.get("/users/", tags=["users"])
async def read_users():
    return [{"username": "johndoe"}]
```

#### Tags with Enums
For large applications, you can use an `Enum` to keep tags consistent: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

```python
from enum import Enum

class Tags(Enum):
    items = "items"
    users = "users"

@app.get("/items/", tags=[Tags.items])
async def get_items():
    return ["Portal gun", "Plumbus"]
```

#### Rich Tag Metadata
You can enrich tags with descriptions and external docs links using `openapi_tags`: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/metadata/]

```python
tags_metadata = [
    {
        "name": "users",
        "description": "Operations with users. The **login** logic is also here.",
    },
    {
        "name": "items",
        "description": "Manage items. So _fancy_ they have their own docs.",
        "externalDocs": {
            "description": "Items external docs",
            "url": "https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/",
        },
    },
]

app = FastAPI(openapi_tags=tags_metadata)
```

Each tag dictionary supports `name` (required), `description` (Markdown supported), and `externalDocs`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/metadata/]

---

### 3. Summary, Description & Docstrings

You can add a `summary` and `description` directly to the decorator: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

```python
@app.post(
    "/items/",
    summary="Create an item",
    description="Create an item with all the information, name, description, price, tax and a set of unique tags",
)
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    return item
```

Or use the function **docstring** for longer descriptions (Markdown is supported): [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

```python
@app.post("/items/", summary="Create an item")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    """
    Create an item with all the information:

    - **name**: each item must have a name
    - **description**: a long description
    - **price**: required
    - **tax**: if the item doesn't have tax, you can omit this
    - **tags**: a set of unique tag strings for this item
    """
    return item
```

You can also use `\f` in the docstring to truncate what FastAPI exposes to OpenAPI (the rest is still available to tools like Sphinx): [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/path-operation-advanced-configuration/]

---

### 4. Response Description & Status Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, status

@app.post(
    "/items/",
    summary="Create an item",
    response_description="The created item",
    status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
)
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    ...
```

`response_description` refers specifically to the response, while `description` refers to the path operation in general. If you don't provide one, FastAPI will automatically generate `"Successful response"`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

The `status_code` will be used in the response and added to the OpenAPI schema. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

---

### 5. Deprecating a Path Operation

Mark an endpoint as deprecated without removing it: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-operation-configuration/]

```python
@app.get("/elements/", tags=["items"], deprecated=True)
async def read_elements():
    return [{"item_id": "Foo"}]
```

---

### 6. Advanced: `openapi_extra`

When you declare a path operation, FastAPI automatically generates the relevant metadata (tags, parameters, requestBody, responses, etc.) to be included in the OpenAPI schema. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/path-operation-advanced-configuration/]

You can extend this with `openapi_extra` for things like OpenAPI Extensions: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/path-operation-advanced-configuration/]

```python
@app.get("/items/", openapi_extra={"x-aperture-labs-portal": "blue"})
async def read_items():
    return [{"item_id": "portal-gun"}]
```

The dictionary in `openapi_extra` will be **deeply merged** with the automatically generated OpenAPI schema for the path operation. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/path-operation-advanced-configuration/]

---

## 📦 Part 2: Validating and Documenting the Request Body

### 1. Declare a Request Body with Pydantic

To declare a request body, use [Pydantic](https://docs.pydantic.dev/) models: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body/]

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    price: float
    tax: float | None = None

@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item):
    return item
```

With just that Python type declaration, FastAPI will: read the body as JSON, convert types, **validate the data** (returning a clear error if invalid), provide editor support, generate JSON Schema definitions, and include those schemas in the OpenAPI docs. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body/]

---

### 2. Field-Level Validation with `Field`

Use Pydantic's `Field` to add per-attribute validation and metadata. Note that `Field` is imported from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-fields/]

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description

question: Why can't FastAPI be faster than Starlette according to the benchmarks?
answer:
Great, the documentation provides a very clear and direct answer to this question. Here it is:

## Why FastAPI Cannot Be Faster Than Starlette

The reason is architectural: **FastAPI is built directly on top of Starlette**, which in turn is built on top of Uvicorn. This creates a strict performance hierarchy:

> **Uvicorn → Starlette → FastAPI**

Each layer can only be **equal to or slower** than the one beneath it, never faster. As the documentation explicitly states:

> *"The same way that Starlette uses Uvicorn and cannot be faster than it, **FastAPI** uses Starlette, so it cannot be faster than it."* [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/benchmarks/]

Here's a breakdown of each layer:

- **Uvicorn** will have the best performance, as it doesn't have much extra code apart from the server itself. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/benchmarks/]
- **Starlette** will have the next best performance after Uvicorn, since it uses Uvicorn to run — it can only get "slower" than Uvicorn by having to execute more code. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/benchmarks/]
- **FastAPI** uses Starlette and adds additional features on top (data validation, serialization, automatic documentation, dependency injection, etc.), so it inherits Starlette's overhead plus its own. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/benchmarks/]

### Important Context for Benchmarks

When comparing benchmarks, it's worth noting that the extra overhead FastAPI adds is not "wasted" — it's the cost of features you'd need to implement yourself anyway. If you used Starlette directly, you'd still have to write your own data validation and serialization, which would add the same (or more) overhead back into your application code. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/benchmarks/]

So the fair comparison for FastAPI is not against raw Starlette or Uvicorn, but against **other full-featured API frameworks** that also provide data validation, serialization, and documentation — such as Flask-apispec, NestJS, or Molten. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/benchmarks/]

question: How do I implement soft deletes in FastAPI with SQLAlchemy?
answer:
The FastAPI documentation does not cover soft deletes as a dedicated topic. However, I can provide a comprehensive, accurate guide by combining the FastAPI + SQLAlchemy/SQLModel patterns documented in the official docs. Here is a complete walkthrough:

---

## Implementing Soft Deletes in FastAPI with SQLAlchemy

> **Note:** The FastAPI documentation does not cover soft deletes directly. However, it provides all the building blocks needed — SQLAlchemy/SQLModel models, session dependencies, PATCH/DELETE endpoints, and partial updates — which we can combine to implement this pattern.

---

### What is a Soft Delete?

A **soft delete** means you don't physically remove a row from the database. Instead, you mark it as deleted (e.g., with a `deleted_at` timestamp or an `is_deleted` boolean flag) and filter it out of normal queries. This preserves data for auditing, recovery, or compliance purposes.

---

### Step 1: Add a `deleted_at` Field to Your Model

FastAPI recommends using **SQLModel** (built on top of SQLAlchemy) for SQL databases. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] You add a nullable `deleted_at` column to your model to track soft deletion:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Annotated, Optional

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, Query
from sqlmodel import Field, Session, SQLModel, create_engine, select


class Hero(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    name: str = Field(index=True)
    age: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, index=True)
    secret_name: str
    deleted_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(default=None)  # <-- soft delete field
```

---

### Step 2: Set Up the Engine and Session Dependency

A SQLModel `engine` (underneath it's actually a SQLAlchemy `engine`) is what **holds the connections** to the database. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/]

A **`Session`** stores objects in memory and keeps track of changes, then uses the `engine` to communicate with the database. You create a FastAPI **dependency** with `yield` that provides a new `Session` for each request. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/]

```python
sqlite_url = "sqlite:///database.db"
connect_args = {"check_same_thread": False}
engine = create_engine(sqlite_url, connect_args=connect_args)


def create_db_and_tables():
    SQLModel.metadata.create_all(engine)


def get_session():
    with Session(engine) as session:
        yield session


SessionDep = Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)]

app = FastAPI()


@app.on_event("startup")
def on_startup():
    create_db_and_tables()
```

Only the code prior to and including the `yield` statement is executed before creating a response; the code after `yield` runs after the response is sent. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/dependencies-with-yield/]

---

### Step 3: The Soft Delete Endpoint

Instead of calling `session.delete(hero)`, you simply **update** the `deleted_at` field with the current timestamp. The standard hard-delete pattern from the docs calls `session.delete()` and `session.commit()` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] — for soft deletes, you replace that with a field update:

```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@app.delete("/heroes/{hero_id}")
def delete_hero(hero_id: int, session: SessionDep):
    hero = session.get(Hero, hero_id)
    if not hero:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")
    if hero.deleted_at is not None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")  # already deleted

    # Soft delete: mark as deleted instead of removing the row
    hero.deleted_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    session.add(hero)
    session.commit()
    return {"ok": True}
```

---

### Step 4: Filter Out Soft-Deleted Records in Read Endpoints

All read queries must be updated to exclude soft-deleted rows by filtering on `deleted_at IS NULL`:

```python
@app.get("/heroes/", response_model=list[HeroPublic])
def read_heroes(
    session: SessionDep,
    offset: int = 0,
    limit: Annotated[int, Query(le=100)] = 100,
):
    # Only return records that have NOT been soft-deleted
    heroes = session.exec(
        select(Hero)
        .where(Hero.deleted_at == None)
        .offset(offset)
        .limit(limit)
    ).all()
    return heroes


@app.get("/heroes/{hero_id}", response_model=HeroPublic)
def read_hero(hero_id: int, session: SessionDep):
    hero = session.get(Hero, hero_id)
    if not hero or hero.deleted_at is not None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")
    return hero
```

---

### Step 5: (Optional) Separate Public and Internal Models

The FastAPI docs recommend using multiple models to control what data is exposed. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] You can create a `HeroPublic` model that omits the `deleted_at` field from API responses:

```python
class HeroBase(SQLModel):
    name: str = Field(index=True)
    age: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, index=True)

class Hero(HeroBase, table=True):
    id: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    secret_name: str
    deleted_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(default=None)

class HeroPublic(HeroBase):
    id: int
    # deleted_at is intentionally excluded from the public schema
```

---

### Step 6: (Optional) Restore a Soft-Deleted Record

You can add a restore endpoint using a `PATCH` request. The docs describe partial updates using `PATCH` and `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` to update only the fields provided. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

```python
@app.patch("/heroes/{hero_id}/restore", response_model=HeroPublic)
def restore_hero(hero_id: int, session: SessionDep):
    hero = session.get(Hero, hero_id)
    if not hero:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")
    if hero.deleted_at is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Hero is not deleted")

    hero.deleted_at = None  # Clear the soft-delete flag
    session.add(hero)
    session.commit()
    session.refresh(hero)
    return hero
```

---

### Full Summary

| Concern | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Model** | Add a `deleted_at: Optional[datetime]` column |
| **Soft Delete** | Set `deleted_at = datetime.now(...)` instead of `session.delete()` |
| **Read queries** | Always filter `.where(Hero.deleted_at == None)` |
| **404 handling** | Treat soft-deleted records as not found |
| **Restore** | Set `deleted_at = None` via a `PATCH` endpoint |
| **Session management** | Use a `yield`-based dependency for one session per request [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] |
| **Response model** | Use a separate `HeroPublic` model that excludes `deleted_at` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] |

This pattern keeps your data intact while making deleted records invisible to normal API consumers.

**FastAPI** doesn't require you to use a SQL (relational) database. But you can use **any database** that you want.

Here we'll see an example using [SQLModel](https://sqlmodel.tiangolo.com/).

**SQLModel** is built on top of [SQLAlchemy](https://www.sqlalchemy.org/) and Pydantic. It was made by the same author of **FastAPI** to be the perfect match for FastAPI applications that need to use **SQL databases**.

/// tip

You could use any other SQL or NoSQL database library you want (in some cases called <abbr title="Object Relational Mapper: a fancy term for a library where some classes represent SQL tables and instances represent rows in those tables">"ORMs"</abbr>), FastAPI doesn't force you to use anything. 😎

///

As SQLModel is based on SQLAlchemy, you can easily use **any database supported** by SQLAlchemy (which makes them also supported by SQLModel), like:

* PostgreSQL
* MySQL
* SQLite
* Oracle
* Microsoft SQL Server, etc.

In this example, we'll use **SQLite**, because it uses a single file and Python has integrated support. So, you can copy this example and run it as is.

Later, for your production application, you might want to use a database server like **PostgreSQL**.

/// tip

There is an official project generator with **FastAPI** and **PostgreSQL** including a frontend and more tools: [https://github.com/fastapi/full-stack-fastapi-template](https://github.com/fastapi/full-stack-fastapi-template)

///

This is a very simple and short tutorial, if you want to learn about databases in general, about SQL, or more advanced features, go to the [SQLModel docs](https://sqlmodel.tiangolo.com/).

# Features { #features }

**FastAPI** gives you the following:

# FastAPI People



FastAPI has an amazing community that welcomes people from all backgrounds.

# OpenAPI `models`



OpenAPI Pydantic models used to generate and validate the generated OpenAPI.

::: fastapi.openapi.models

# Body - Updates { #body-updates }

## Partial updates with `PATCH` { #partial-updates-with-patch }

### Partial updates recap { #partial-updates-recap }

In summary, to apply partial updates you would:

* (Optionally) use `PATCH` instead of `PUT`.

* Retrieve the stored data.

* Put that data in a Pydantic model.

* Generate a `dict` without default values from the input model (using `exclude_unset`).

    * This way you can update only the values actually set by the user, instead of overriding values already stored with default values in your model.

* Create a copy of the stored model, updating its attributes with the received partial updates (using the `update` parameter).

* Convert the copied model to something that can be stored in your DB (for example, using the `jsonable_encoder`).

    * This is comparable to using the model's `.model_dump()` method again, but it makes sure (and converts) the values to data types that can be converted to JSON, for example, `datetime` to `str`.

* Save the data to your DB.

* Return the updated model.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    price: float | None = None
    tax: float = 10.5
    tags: list[str] = []


items = {
    "foo": {"name": "Foo", "price": 50.2},
    "bar": {"name": "Bar", "description": "The bartenders", "price": 62, "tax": 20.2},
    "baz": {"name": "Baz", "description": None, "price": 50.2, "tax": 10.5, "tags": []},
}


@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    return items[item_id]


@app.patch("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(item_id: str, item: Item) -> Item:
    stored_item_data = items[item_id]
    stored_item_model = Item(**stored_item_data)
    update_data = item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    updated_item = stored_item_model.model_copy(update=update_data)
    items[item_id] = jsonable_encoder(updated_item)
    return updated_item

# Dependencies with yield { #dependencies-with-yield }

## A database dependency with `yield` { #a-database-dependency-with-yield }



For example, you could use this to create a database session and close it after finishing.

Only the code prior to and including the `yield` statement is executed before creating a response:

```python
async def get_db():
    db = DBSession()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
```

The yielded value is what is injected into *path operations* and other dependencies:

```python
async def get_db():
    db = DBSession()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
```

The code following the `yield` statement is executed after the response:

```python
async def get_db():
    db = DBSession()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
```

You can use `async` or regular functions.

**FastAPI** will do the right thing with each, the same as with normal dependencies.

answer_raw:
The FastAPI documentation does not cover soft deletes as a dedicated topic. However, I can provide a comprehensive, accurate guide by combining the FastAPI + SQLAlchemy/SQLModel patterns documented in the official docs. Here is a complete walkthrough:

---

## Implementing Soft Deletes in FastAPI with SQLAlchemy

> **Note:** The FastAPI documentation does not cover soft deletes directly. However, it provides all the building blocks needed — SQLAlchemy/SQLModel models, session dependencies, PATCH/DELETE endpoints, and partial updates — which we can combine to implement this pattern.

---

### What is a Soft Delete?

A **soft delete** means you don't physically remove a row from the database. Instead, you mark it as deleted (e.g., with a `deleted_at` timestamp or an `is_deleted` boolean flag) and filter it out of normal queries. This preserves data for auditing, recovery, or compliance purposes.

---

### Step 1: Add a `deleted_at` Field to Your Model

FastAPI recommends using **SQLModel** (built on top of SQLAlchemy) for SQL databases. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] You add a nullable `deleted_at` column to your model to track soft deletion:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Annotated, Optional

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, Query
from sqlmodel import Field, Session, SQLModel, create_engine, select


class Hero(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    name: str = Field(index=True)
    age: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, index=True)
    secret_name: str
    deleted_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(default=None)  # <-- soft delete field
```

---

### Step 2: Set Up the Engine and Session Dependency

A SQLModel `engine` (underneath it's actually a SQLAlchemy `engine`) is what **holds the connections** to the database. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/]

A **`Session`** stores objects in memory and keeps track of changes, then uses the `engine` to communicate with the database. You create a FastAPI **dependency** with `yield` that provides a new `Session` for each request. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/]

```python
sqlite_url = "sqlite:///database.db"
connect_args = {"check_same_thread": False}
engine = create_engine(sqlite_url, connect_args=connect_args)


def create_db_and_tables():
    SQLModel.metadata.create_all(engine)


def get_session():
    with Session(engine) as session:
        yield session


SessionDep = Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)]

app = FastAPI()


@app.on_event("startup")
def on_startup():
    create_db_and_tables()
```

Only the code prior to and including the `yield` statement is executed before creating a response; the code after `yield` runs after the response is sent. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/dependencies-with-yield/]

---

### Step 3: The Soft Delete Endpoint

Instead of calling `session.delete(hero)`, you simply **update** the `deleted_at` field with the current timestamp. The standard hard-delete pattern from the docs calls `session.delete()` and `session.commit()` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] — for soft deletes, you replace that with a field update:

```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@app.delete("/heroes/{hero_id}")
def delete_hero(hero_id: int, session: SessionDep):
    hero = session.get(Hero, hero_id)
    if not hero:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")
    if hero.deleted_at is not None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")  # already deleted

    # Soft delete: mark as deleted instead of removing the row
    hero.deleted_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    session.add(hero)
    session.commit()
    return {"ok": True}
```

---

### Step 4: Filter Out Soft-Deleted Records in Read Endpoints

All read queries must be updated to exclude soft-deleted rows by filtering on `deleted_at IS NULL`:

```python
@app.get("/heroes/", response_model=list[HeroPublic])
def read_heroes(
    session: SessionDep,
    offset: int = 0,
    limit: Annotated[int, Query(le=100)] = 100,
):
    # Only return records that have NOT been soft-deleted
    heroes = session.exec(
        select(Hero)
        .where(Hero.deleted_at == None)
        .offset(offset)
        .limit(limit)
    ).all()
    return heroes


@app.get("/heroes/{hero_id}", response_model=HeroPublic)
def read_hero(hero_id: int, session: SessionDep):
    hero = session.get(Hero, hero_id)
    if not hero or hero.deleted_at is not None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")
    return hero
```

---

### Step 5: (Optional) Separate Public and Internal Models

The FastAPI docs recommend using multiple models to control what data is exposed. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] You can create a `HeroPublic` model that omits the `deleted_at` field from API responses:

```python
class HeroBase(SQLModel):
    name: str = Field(index=True)
    age: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, index=True)

class Hero(HeroBase, table=True):
    id: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    secret_name: str
    deleted_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(default=None)

class HeroPublic(HeroBase):
    id: int
    # deleted_at is intentionally excluded from the public schema
```

---

### Step 6: (Optional) Restore a Soft-Deleted Record

You can add a restore endpoint using a `PATCH` request. The docs describe partial updates using `PATCH` and `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` to update only the fields provided. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

```python
@app.patch("/heroes/{hero_id}/restore", response_model=HeroPublic)
def restore_hero(hero_id: int, session: SessionDep):
    hero = session.get(Hero, hero_id)
    if not hero:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Hero not found")
    if hero.deleted_at is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Hero is not deleted")

    hero.deleted_at = None  # Clear the soft-delete flag
    session.add(hero)
    session.commit()
    session.refresh(hero)
    return hero
```

---

### Full Summary

| Concern | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Model** | Add a `deleted_at: Optional[datetime]` column |
| **Soft Delete** | Set `deleted_at = datetime.now(...)` instead of `session.delete()` |
| **Read queries** | Always filter `.where(Hero.deleted_at == None)` |
| **404 handling** | Treat soft-deleted records as not found |
| **Restore** | Set `deleted_at = None` via a `PATCH` endpoint |
| **Session management** | Use a `yield`-based dependency for one session per request [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] |
| **Response model** | Use a separate `HeroPublic` model that excludes `deleted_at` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/] |

This pattern keeps your data intact while making deleted records invisible to normal API consumers.

question: Where can you see the schemas for the data to be sent in requests and received in responses when using FastAPI?
answer:
In FastAPI, you can see the schemas for request and response data in **three places**:

---

### 1. 🖥️ Swagger UI — Interactive API Docs (`/docs`)
FastAPI automatically generates interactive API documentation powered by **Swagger UI**, accessible at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/] This UI lets you explore and even test your API directly from the browser, and it displays the schemas for all request bodies and responses. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/features/]

---

### 2. 📄 ReDoc — Alternative API Docs (`/redoc`)
FastAPI also includes an alternative documentation UI using **ReDoc**, which also displays the data schemas in a clean, readable format. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/features/]

---

### 3. 🔧 Raw OpenAPI JSON (`/openapi.json`)
FastAPI automatically generates a raw **OpenAPI JSON schema** that describes all your API paths, parameters, request bodies, and responses. You can view it directly at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/first-steps/]

This JSON schema is what powers both documentation UIs mentioned above. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/first-steps/]

---

### How are the schemas generated?
FastAPI generates **JSON Schema** definitions for your data models (defined with Pydantic), and these schemas become part of the generated OpenAPI schema, which is then used by the automatic documentation UIs. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body/] FastAPI is fully based on the open standards **OpenAPI** and **JSON Schema**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/]

question: How do I add rate limiting to FastAPI using the slowapi package?
answer:
The FastAPI documentation does not cover `slowapi` directly, as it is a third-party package. However, the docs do cover the underlying FastAPI/Starlette concepts (middleware, exception handlers, ASGI middleware) that `slowapi` builds upon. I'll use those documented concepts alongside well-established `slowapi` usage patterns to give you a complete, accurate guide.

---

## Adding Rate Limiting to FastAPI with `slowapi`

`slowapi` is a popular third-party rate-limiting library for FastAPI/Starlette. It is inspired by Flask-Limiter and integrates cleanly with FastAPI's middleware and exception handler system.

---

### 1. Install the packages

```bash
pip install slowapi
```

---

### 2. How it integrates with FastAPI

FastAPI is based on Starlette and implements the ASGI specification, so you can use any ASGI-compatible middleware or extension. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/]

`slowapi` plugs in via:
- **`app.state`** — to attach the `Limiter` instance to the app
- **`app.add_middleware()`** — to add the `SlowAPIMiddleware` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/]
- **`@app.exception_handler()`** — to handle rate-limit-exceeded errors [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/]

---

### 3. Full working example

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from slowapi import Limiter, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address
from slowapi.errors import RateLimitExceeded
from slowapi.middleware import SlowAPIMiddleware

# 1. Create a Limiter instance, keyed by the client's IP address
limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)

app = FastAPI()

# 2. Attach the limiter to the app's state
app.state.limiter = limiter

# 3. Register the rate-limit-exceeded exception handler
#    so FastAPI returns a proper 429 response
app.add_exception_handler(RateLimitExceeded, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler)

# 4. Add the SlowAPI middleware
app.add_middleware(SlowAPIMiddleware)


# 5. Apply rate limits to individual routes using the @limiter.limit decorator
@app.get("/")
@limiter.limit("5/minute")  # Allow 5 requests per minute per IP
async def homepage(request: Request):
    return {"message": "Hello, World!"}


@app.get("/items")
@limiter.limit("10/minute")  # Different limit for this route
async def get_items(request: Request):
    return {"items": ["item1", "item2"]}
```

---

### 4. Key concepts explained

#### Middleware (`app.add_middleware`)
A middleware intercepts every request before it reaches your path operation and every response before it's returned. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/middleware/] `SlowAPIMiddleware` uses this to track and enforce request counts.

FastAPI's `app.add_middleware()` accepts a middleware class as the first argument and any additional keyword arguments to pass to it. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/]

#### Exception Handler (`app.add_exception_handler`)
When a rate limit is exceeded, `slowapi` raises a `RateLimitExceeded` exception. You register a custom handler for it so FastAPI returns a clean `429 Too Many Requests` response. FastAPI allows you to add custom exception handlers with `@app.exception_handler()` or `app.add_exception_handler()`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/]

#### The `request: Request` parameter
The `request` parameter **must** be present in your route function signature for `slowapi` to work. FastAPI provides `Request` from `fastapi` (which comes directly from Starlette). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/middleware/]

---

### 5. Rate limit string formats

`slowapi` supports flexible limit strings:

| Format | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"5/minute"` | 5 requests per minute |
| `"100/hour"` | 100 requests per hour |
| `"1000/day"` | 1000 requests per day |
| `"5/minute;100/hour"` | Multiple limits combined |

---

### 6. Global default limits (optional)

You can set a default limit for all routes at the `Limiter` level:

```python
limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address, default_limits=["100/minute"])
```

Individual routes can then override this with their own `@limiter.limit(...)` decorator.

---

### 7. Using a custom key function

Instead of limiting by IP, you can limit by any request attribute (e.g., API key, user ID):

```python
def get_api_key(request: Request):
    return request.headers.get("X-API-Key", get_remote_address(request))

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_api_key)
```

---

### Summary

| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| Install | `pip install slowapi` |
| Create limiter | `Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)` |
| Attach to app | `app.state.limiter = limiter` |
| Add middleware | `app.add_middleware(SlowAPIMiddleware)` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/] |
| Handle errors | `app.add_exception_handler(RateLimitExceeded, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler)` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/] |
| Decorate routes | `@limiter.limit("5/minute")` |

> **Note:** The FastAPI official documentation does not cover `slowapi` directly, as it is a third-party package. The integration patterns above are based on `slowapi`'s own documentation and FastAPI's documented middleware/exception-handler system. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/] [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/]

You can add middleware to **FastAPI** applications.

A "middleware" is a function that works with every **request** before it is processed by any specific *path operation*. And also with every **response** before returning it.

* Then it returns the **response**.

# CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) { #cors-cross-origin-resource-sharing }

## Use `CORSMiddleware` { #use-corsmiddleware }

You can configure it in your **FastAPI** application using the `CORSMiddleware`.

* Import `CORSMiddleware`.

* Create a list of allowed origins (as strings).

* Add it as a "middleware" to your **FastAPI** application.

You can also specify whether your backend allows:

* Credentials (Authorization headers, Cookies, etc).

* Specific HTTP methods (`POST`, `PUT`) or all of them with the wildcard `"*"`.

* Specific HTTP headers or all of them with the wildcard `"*"`.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app = FastAPI()

origins = [
    "http://localhost.tiangolo.com",
    "https://localhost.tiangolo.com",
    "http://localhost",
    "http://localhost:8080",
]

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=origins,
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)


@app.get("/")
async def main():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}
```

The default parameters used by the `CORSMiddleware` implementation are restrictive by default, so you'll need to explicitly enable particular origins, methods, or headers, in order for browsers to be permitted to use them in a Cross-Domain context.

The following arguments are supported:

* `allow_origins` - A list of origins that should be permitted to make cross-origin requests. E.g. `['https://example.org', 'https://www.example.org']`. You can use `['*']` to allow any origin.

* `allow_origin_regex` - A regex string to match against origins that should be permitted to make cross-origin requests. e.g. `'https://.*\.example\.org'`.

* `allow_methods` - A list of HTTP methods that should be allowed for cross-origin requests. Defaults to `['GET']`. You can use `['*']` to allow all standard methods.

`slowapi` plugs in via:
- **`app.state`** — to attach the `Limiter` instance to the app
- **`app.add_middleware()`** — to add the `SlowAPIMiddleware` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/]
- **`@app.exception_handler()`** — to handle rate-limit-exceeded errors [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/]

---

### 3. Full working example

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from slowapi import Limiter, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address
from slowapi.errors import RateLimitExceeded
from slowapi.middleware import SlowAPIMiddleware

# 1. Create a Limiter instance, keyed by the client's IP address
limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)

app = FastAPI()

# 2. Attach the limiter to the app's state
app.state.limiter = limiter

# 3. Register the rate-limit-exceeded exception handler
#    so FastAPI returns a proper 429 response
app.add_exception_handler(RateLimitExceeded, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler)

# 4. Add the SlowAPI middleware
app.add_middleware(SlowAPIMiddleware)


# 5. Apply rate limits to individual routes using the @limiter.limit decorator
@app.get("/")
@limiter.limit("5/minute")  # Allow 5 requests per minute per IP
async def homepage(request: Request):
    return {"message": "Hello, World!"}


@app.get("/items")
@limiter.limit("10/minute")  # Different limit for this route
async def get_items(request: Request):
    return {"items": ["item1", "item2"]}
```

---

### 4. Key concepts explained

#### Middleware (`app.add_middleware`)
A middleware intercepts every request before it reaches your path operation and every response before it's returned. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/middleware/] `SlowAPIMiddleware` uses this to track and enforce request counts.

FastAPI's `app.add_middleware()` accepts a middleware class as the first argument and any additional keyword arguments to pass to it. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/]

#### Exception Handler (`app.add_exception_handler`)
When a rate limit is exceeded, `slowapi` raises a `RateLimitExceeded` exception. You register a custom handler for it so FastAPI returns a clean `429 Too Many Requests` response. FastAPI allows you to add custom exception handlers with `@app.exception_handler()` or `app.add_exception_handler()`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/]

#### The `request: Request` parameter
The `request` parameter **must** be present in your route function signature for `slowapi` to work. FastAPI provides `Request` from `fastapi` (which comes directly from Starlette). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/middleware/]

---

### 5. Rate limit string formats

`slowapi` supports flexible limit strings:

| Format | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"5/minute"` | 5 requests per minute |
| `"100/hour"` | 100 requests per hour |
| `"1000/day"` | 1000 requests per day |
| `"5/minute;100/hour"` | Multiple limits combined |

---

### 6. Global default limits (optional)

You can set a default limit for all routes at the `Limiter` level:

```python
limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address, default_limits=["100/minute"])
```

Individual routes can then override this with their own `@limiter.limit(...)` decorator.

---

### 7. Using a custom key function

Instead of limiting by IP, you can limit by any request attribute (e.g., API key, user ID):

```python
def get_api_key(request: Request):
    return request.headers.get("X-API-Key", get_remote_address(request))

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_api_key)
```

---

### Summary

| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| Install | `pip install slowapi` |
| Create limiter | `Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)` |
| Attach to app | `app.state.limiter = limiter` |
| Add middleware | `app.add_middleware(SlowAPIMiddleware)` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/] |
| Handle errors | `app.add_exception_handler(RateLimitExceeded, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler)` [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/] |
| Decorate routes | `@limiter.limit("5/minute")` |

> **Note:** The FastAPI official documentation does not cover `slowapi` directly, as it is a third-party package. The integration patterns above are based on `slowapi`'s own documentation and FastAPI's documented middleware/exception-handler system. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/middleware/] [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/]

question: What do the improved method names in the generated TypeScript client include?
answer:
Based on the retrieved documentation, here is a detailed answer about the improved method names in the generated TypeScript client:

The improved method names in the generated TypeScript client include **the tag** and then the **function name (path operation name)**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/]

Specifically, they **no longer include** information from the URL path and the HTTP operation. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/]

### Background

By default, the client generator uses the OpenAPI internal **operation ID** for each path operation to generate method names. FastAPI generates these operation IDs using the **function name**, the **path**, and the **HTTP method/operation** to ensure uniqueness — resulting in messy names like `createItemItemsPost`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/]

### How the Improvement Works

To get cleaner method names, you can customize how operation IDs are generated so they are based on the **tag** and the **path operation function name** only. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/]

Additionally, you can further preprocess the OpenAPI specification to **remove the prefixed tag** from the operation IDs (e.g., renaming `items-get_items` to just `get_items`), so the client generator produces even simpler and cleaner method names. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/]

The end result is a generated client with **clean method names**, full **autocompletion**, and **inline errors**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/]

question: What is the term used to refer to the object returned by an `async def` function in FastAPI?
answer:
The term used to refer to the object returned by an `async def` function in FastAPI is a **Coroutine**.

As the FastAPI documentation explains:

> **"Coroutine"** is just the very fancy term for the thing returned by an `async def` function. Python knows that it is something like a function, that it can start and that it will end at some point, but that it might be paused ⏸ internally too, whenever there is an `await` inside of it. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/]

In other words, when you define a function with `async def`, calling it returns a **coroutine** object. All the functionality of using asynchronous code with `async` and `await` is summarized as using "coroutines", which is comparable to the main key feature of Go — the "Goroutines". [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/]

question: What is the return type of the `read_item` function in the FastAPI example?
answer:
The `read_item` function appears in **multiple examples** across the FastAPI documentation, and its return type varies depending on the context. Here are the key examples:

---

### 1. Path Parameters Example
In the **Path Parameters** tutorial, `read_item` has **no explicit return type annotation** and simply returns a dictionary:

```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    return {"item_id": item_id}
```
The function returns a plain `dict` (e.g., `{"item_id": 3}`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params/]

---

### 2. Query Parameters Example
In the **Query Parameters** tutorial, `read_item` also has **no explicit return type annotation** and returns a dictionary built dynamically:

```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: str, q: str | None = None, short: bool = False):
    item = {"item_id": item_id}
    ...
    return item
```
Again, the return type is an implicit `dict`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-params/]

---

### 3. Response Model Example
In the **Response Model** tutorial, `read_item` uses a `response_model=Item` in the decorator (with `response_model_exclude_unset=True`) and has **no explicit return type annotation**:

```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude_unset=True)
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    return items[item_id]
```
Here, the effective response type is the Pydantic `Item` model, declared via the `response_model` parameter rather than a return type annotation. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/response-model/]

---

### Summary
In the most basic FastAPI example (Path Parameters), `read_item` returns a **`dict`** with no explicit return type annotation. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params/] In more advanced examples, the return type is governed by a **Pydantic `Item` model**, either via a return type annotation or the `response_model` parameter on the route decorator. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/response-model/]

# Query Parameters { #query-parameters }

## Query parameter type conversion { #query-parameter-type-conversion }



You can also declare `bool` types, and they will be converted:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: str, q: str | None = None, short: bool = False):
    item = {"item_id": item_id}
    if q:
        item.update({"q": q})
    if not short:
        item.update(
            {"description": "This is an amazing item that has a long description"}
        )
    return item
```

In this case, if you go to:

```
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo?short=1
```

or

```
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo?short=True
```

or

```
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo?short=true
```

or

```
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo?short=on
```

or

```
http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/foo?short=yes
```

or any other case variation (uppercase, first letter in uppercase, etc), your function will see the parameter `short` with a `bool` value of `True`. Otherwise as `False`.

## Results { #results }



With just that Python type declaration, **FastAPI** will:

* Read the body of the request as JSON.
* Convert the corresponding types (if needed).
* Validate the data.
    * If the data is invalid, it will return a nice and clear error, indicating exactly where and what was the incorrect data.
* Give you the received data in the parameter `item`.
    * As you declared it in the function to be of type `Item`, you will also have all the editor support (completion, etc) for all of the attributes and their types.
* Generate [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org) definitions for your model, you can also use them anywhere else you like if it makes sense for your project.
* Those schemas will be part of the generated OpenAPI schema, and used by the automatic documentation <abbr title="User Interfaces">UIs</abbr>.

question: How do you create a copy of an existing Pydantic model with updated data in FastAPI?
answer:
Here is a comprehensive explanation of how to create a copy of an existing Pydantic model with updated data in FastAPI:

---

## Copying a Pydantic Model with Updated Data

In FastAPI (with **Pydantic v2**), you use the **`.model_copy(update=...)`** method to create a copy of an existing model instance with specific fields updated.

---

### The Method: `.model_copy(update=update_data)`

You can create a copy of the existing model using `.model_copy()`, and pass the `update` parameter with a `dict` containing the data to update. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

```python
updated_item = stored_item_model.model_copy(update=update_data)
```

---

### Full Example (Partial Updates with `PATCH`)

This pattern is most commonly used for partial updates. Here's the complete workflow: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    price: float | None = None
    tax: float = 10.5
    tags: list[str] = []


items = {
    "foo": {"name": "Foo", "price": 50.2},
    "bar": {"name": "Bar", "description": "The bartenders", "price": 62, "tax": 20.2},
    "baz": {"name": "Baz", "description": None, "price": 50.2, "tax": 10.5, "tags": []},
}


@app.patch("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(item_id: str, item: Item) -> Item:
    stored_item_data = items[item_id]           # 1. Retrieve stored data
    stored_item_model = Item(**stored_item_data) # 2. Load into Pydantic model
    update_data = item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)  # 3. Get only fields the user sent
    updated_item = stored_item_model.model_copy(update=update_data)  # 4. Copy with updates
    items[item_id] = jsonable_encoder(updated_item)    # 5. Store it
    return updated_item                                # 6. Return updated model
```

---

### Step-by-Step Breakdown

To apply partial updates correctly, you would: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

1. **Retrieve the stored data** from your database or storage.
2. **Put that data in a Pydantic model** (e.g., `Item(**stored_item_data)`).
3. **Generate a `dict` without default values** from the input model using `exclude_unset=True` — this way you only update the values actually set by the user, instead of overriding stored values with model defaults. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
4. **Create a copy of the stored model** with the received partial updates using `.model_copy(update=update_data)`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
5. **Convert the copied model** to a JSON-compatible format using `jsonable_encoder` (e.g., converts `datetime` to `str`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
6. **Save and return** the updated model.

---

### Key Points

- **`.model_copy(update=...)`** is the Pydantic v2 method for this. It takes a `dict` of fields to override in the copy. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
- **`.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)`** is critical — it generates a `dict` with only the data that was explicitly set when creating the model, excluding default values, so you don't accidentally overwrite stored data with defaults. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
- The input model is **still validated** by FastAPI/Pydantic, so if you want to receive partial updates that can omit all attributes, you need a model where all attributes are marked as optional (with default values or `None`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

# Release Notes

## 0.100.0 (2023-07-07)

### Migration



Check out the [Pydantic migration guide](https://docs.pydantic.dev/2.0/migration/).

For the things that need changes in your Pydantic models, the Pydantic team built [`bump-pydantic`](https://github.com/pydantic/bump-pydantic).

A command line tool that will **process your code** and update most of the things **automatically** for you. Make sure you have your code in git first, and review each of the changes to make sure everything is correct before committing the changes.

# Python Types Intro { #python-types-intro }

## Pydantic models { #pydantic-models }



[Pydantic](https://docs.pydantic.dev/) is a Python library to perform data validation.

You declare the "shape" of the data as classes with attributes.

And each attribute has a type.

Then you create an instance of that class with some values and it will validate the values, convert them to the appropriate type (if that's the case) and give you an object with all the data.

And you get all the editor support with that resulting object.

An example from the official Pydantic docs:

```python
from datetime import datetime

from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str = "John Doe"
    signup_ts: datetime | None = None
    friends: list[int] = []


external_data = {
    "id": "123",
    "signup_ts": "2017-06-01 12:22",
    "friends": [1, "2", b"3"],
}
user = User(**external_data)
print(user)
# > User id=123 name='John Doe' signup_ts=datetime.datetime(2017, 6, 1, 12, 22) friends=[1, 2, 3]
print(user.id)
# > 123
```

/// note

To learn more about [Pydantic, check its docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev/).

///

**FastAPI** is all based on Pydantic.

You will see a lot more of all this in practice in the [Tutorial - User Guide](tutorial/index.md).

# Features { #features }

## Pydantic features { #pydantic-features }



**FastAPI** is fully compatible with (and based on) [**Pydantic**](https://docs.pydantic.dev/). So, any additional Pydantic code you have, will also work.

Including external libraries also based on Pydantic, such as <abbr title="Object-Relational Mapper">ORM</abbr>s and <abbr title="Object-Document Mapper">ODM</abbr>s for databases.

This also means that in many cases you can pass the same object you get from a request **directly to the database**, as everything is validated automatically.

The same applies the other way around, in many cases you can just pass the object you get from the database **directly to the client**.

With **FastAPI** you get all of **Pydantic**'s features (as FastAPI is based on Pydantic for all the data handling):

* **No brainfuck**:
    * No new schema definition micro-language to learn.
    * If you know Python types you know how to use Pydantic.
* Plays nicely with your **<abbr title="Integrated Development Environment: similar to a code editor">IDE</abbr>/<dfn title="A program that checks for code errors">linter</dfn>/brain**:
    * Because pydantic data structures are just instances of classes you define; auto-completion, linting, mypy and your intuition should all work properly with your validated data.
* Validate **complex structures**:
    * Use of hierarchical Pydantic models, Python `typing`’s `List` and `Dict`, etc.
    * And validators allow complex data schemas to be clearly and easily defined, checked and documented as JSON Schema.
    * You can have deeply **nested JSON** objects and have them all validated and annotated.
* **Extensible**:
    * Pydantic allows custom data types to be defined or you can extend validation with methods on a model decorated with the validator decorator.
* 100% test coverage.

To apply partial updates correctly, you would: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

1. **Retrieve the stored data** from your database or storage.
2. **Put that data in a Pydantic model** (e.g., `Item(**stored_item_data)`).
3. **Generate a `dict` without default values** from the input model using `exclude_unset=True` — this way you only update the values actually set by the user, instead of overriding stored values with model defaults. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
4. **Create a copy of the stored model** with the received partial updates using `.model_copy(update=update_data)`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
5. **Convert the copied model** to a JSON-compatible format using `jsonable_encoder` (e.g., converts `datetime` to `str`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
6. **Save and return** the updated model.

---

### Key Points

- **`.model_copy(update=...)`** is the Pydantic v2 method for this. It takes a `dict` of fields to override in the copy. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
- **`.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)`** is critical — it generates a `dict` with only the data that was explicitly set when creating the model, excluding default values, so you don't accidentally overwrite stored data with defaults. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]
- The input model is **still validated** by FastAPI/Pydantic, so if you want to receive partial updates that can omit all attributes, you need a model where all attributes are marked as optional (with default values or `None`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-updates/]

question: What package must be installed to receive uploaded files and/or form data in FastAPI?
answer:
To receive uploaded files and/or form data in FastAPI, you must install the **`python-multipart`** package.

You can install it with the following command:

```console
$ pip install python-multipart
```

This requirement applies in all related scenarios:

- **Receiving uploaded files**: `python-multipart` must be installed because uploaded files are sent as "form data". [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/request-files/]
- **Receiving form data**: `python-multipart` is also required when using `Form` fields. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/request-forms/]
- **Receiving both files and form fields together**: The same `python-multipart` package is needed when using `File` and `Form` simultaneously. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/request-forms-and-files/]

- Your API docs will be available at **`http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/]

```

question: How can I use FastAPI with lifespan management for testing while also configuring it to run behind a proxy with a specific root path?
answer:
I now have all the information needed to give a comprehensive, well-cited answer. Here it is:

---

## Using FastAPI with Lifespan Management for Testing + Behind a Proxy with `root_path`

These two features are completely independent of each other and can be combined cleanly. Let's cover each in depth, then show how to put them together.

---

## Part 1: Lifespan Management

### What is it?

The lifespan feature lets you define **startup** and **shutdown** logic in a single function. It's useful for setting up shared resources (e.g., DB connections, ML models) before the app starts taking requests, and cleaning them up on shutdown. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/events/]

### How to define it

You create an `async` function decorated with `@asynccontextmanager`. Code **before** the `yield` runs at startup; code **after** the `yield` runs at shutdown. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/events/]

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI

ml_models = {}

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # --- STARTUP: runs before the app starts taking requests ---
    ml_models["predictor"] = lambda x: x * 42
    yield
    # --- SHUTDOWN: runs after the app finishes handling requests ---
    ml_models.clear()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

@app.get("/predict")
async def predict(x: float):
    result = ml_models["predictor"](x)
    return {"result": result}
```

The `lifespan` parameter of the `FastAPI` app takes an **async context manager**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/events/]

> ⚠️ **Note:** The deprecated `@app.on_event("startup")` / `@app.on_event("shutdown")` approach still works but is no longer recommended. If you provide a `lifespan` parameter, those event handlers will no longer be called — it's all `lifespan` or all events, not both. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/events/]

---

## Part 2: Testing with Lifespan

When you need the lifespan to run during tests, use `TestClient` as a **context manager** (i.e., inside a `with` block). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/testing-events/]

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

def test_predict():
    # Before the "with" block: lifespan hasn't started yet
    assert ml_models == {}

    with TestClient(app) as client:
        # Inside the "with" block: lifespan has started, resources are ready
        assert "predictor" in ml_models

        response = client.get("/predict?x=2")
        assert response.status_code == 200
        assert response.json() == {"result": 84.0}

    # After the "with" block: lifespan has ended, resources are cleaned up
    assert ml_models == {}
```

- Entering the `with TestClient(app)` block **triggers the startup** (code before `yield`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/testing-events/]
- Exiting the `with` block **simulates app termination**, triggering the shutdown (code after `yield`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/testing-events/]

---

## Part 3: Running Behind a Proxy with `root_path`

### The Problem

When a proxy (e.g., Nginx, Traefik) strips a path prefix before forwarding requests to your app, your app is unaware of the full public URL. For example, the proxy serves your app at `/api/v1/app`, but your app only knows about `/app`. This breaks the OpenAPI docs UI, which would try to fetch `/openapi.json` instead of `/api/v1/openapi.json`. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/]

### Solution: `root_path`

`root_path` is a mechanism provided by the ASGI specification that FastAPI is built on (through Starlette). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/]

**Option A — Via CLI (recommended for production):**
```console
$ fastapi run main.py --forwarded-allow-ips="*" --root-path /api/v1
```
[https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/]

**Option B — Directly in the `FastAPI` constructor:**
```python
app = FastAPI(root_path="/api/v1")
```
Passing `root_path` to `FastAPI()` is the equivalent of passing the `--root-path` CLI option to Uvicorn or Hypercorn. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/]

### Inspecting `root_path` at runtime

You can read the current `root_path` from the ASGI `scope` on any request: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/]

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

app = FastAPI(root_path="/api/v1")

@app.get("/app")
def read_main(request: Request):
    return {"message": "Hello World", "root_path": request.scope.get("root_path")}
```

### Optional: Disable automatic server from `root_path` in OpenAPI

By default, FastAPI adds the `root_path` as a server entry in the OpenAPI schema. You can disable this with `root_path_in_servers=False`: [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/]

```python
app = FastAPI(
    root_path="/api/v1",
    root_path_in_servers=False,
    servers=[
        {"url": "https://prod.example.com", "description": "Production"},
    ],
)
```

---

## Part 4: Combining Both — Full Example

Here's a complete example that uses **lifespan management**, **proxy `root_path`**, and **lifespan-aware testing** all together:

```python
# main.py
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

ml_models = {}

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup: load resources
    ml_models["predictor"] = lambda x: x * 42
    yield
    # Shutdown: release resources
    ml_models.clear()

app = FastAPI(
    lifespan=lifespan,
    root_path="/api/v1",  # Tells the app it's mounted behind a proxy at /api/v1
)

@app.get("/predict")
async def predict(x: float, request: Request):
    result = ml_models["predictor"](x)
    return {
        "result": result,
        "root_path": request.scope.get("root_path"),
    }
```

```python
# test_main.py
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app, ml_models

def test_predict_with_lifespan():
    # Lifespan hasn't started yet
    assert ml_models == {}

    with TestClient(app) as client:
        # Lifespan is now active — ml_models is populated
        assert "predictor" in ml_models

        response = client.get("/predict?x=3")
        assert response.status_code == 200
        data = response.json()
        assert data["result"] == 126.0
        assert data["root_path"] == "/api/v1"  # root_path is visible in tests too

    # Lifespan has ended — ml_models is cleaned up
    assert ml_models == {}
```

| **Test lifespan events** | Use `with TestClient(app) as client:` — entering starts lifespan, exiting ends it [https

## CSRF Risk { #csrf-risk }



This default behavior provides protection against a class of **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** attacks in a very specific scenario.

These attacks exploit the fact that browsers allow scripts to send requests without doing any CORS preflight check when they:

* don't have a `Content-Type` header (e.g. using `fetch()` with a `Blob` body)
* and don't send any authentication credentials.

This type of attack is mainly relevant when:

* the application is running locally (e.g. on `localhost`) or in an internal network
* and the application doesn't have any authentication, it expects that any request from the same network can be trusted.

question: What must the backend include in its list of allowed origins for the frontend at http://localhost:8080 to work correctly?
answer:
The backend must include **`http://localhost:8080`** in its list of allowed origins.

Here's the full explanation:

- An **origin** is the combination of protocol, domain, and port. For example, `http://localhost`, `https://localhost`, and `http://localhost:8080` are all considered **different origins**, even though they share the same domain (`localhost`). [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/cors/]

- When a frontend running at `http://localhost:8080` tries to communicate with a backend at `http://localhost` (port 80), the browser sends an HTTP `OPTIONS` preflight request to the backend. For the communication to be allowed, the backend must respond with the appropriate CORS headers. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/cors/]

- Specifically, **the backend's list of allowed origins must include `http://localhost:8080`** for the frontend at that origin to work correctly. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/cors/]

In FastAPI, this is configured using the `CORSMiddleware`:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app = FastAPI()

origins = [
    "http://localhost:8080",
]

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=origins,
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
```
[https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/cors/]

> **Note:** While you *can* use the wildcard `"*"` to allow all origins, this will **not** work correctly for requests that involve credentials (e.g., cookies or Authorization headers). It is therefore better to **explicitly specify** the allowed origins. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/cors/]

question: What happens to the data returned in a path operation if a response model is declared and a response class with a JSON media type is used?
answer:
Here is a detailed explanation of what happens to the data returned in a path operation when both a **response model** is declared and a **response class with a JSON media type** is used:

---

## Data Processing with a Response Model + JSON Media Type Response Class

When you declare a `response_class` with a JSON media type (such as `application/json`, like `JSONResponse`), the returned data goes through the following steps:

### 1. Automatic Conversion and Filtering via the Response Model
The data you return will be **automatically converted (and filtered)** using any Pydantic `response_model` declared in the path operation decorator. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/custom-response/]

This means only the fields defined in the `response_model` will be included in the output — extra fields are stripped away. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/response-model/]

### 2. Serialization via `jsonable_encoder`, NOT Pydantic Directly
Even though the response model is used for filtering, the data is **not** serialized to JSON bytes by Pydantic directly. Instead, it is first converted using `jsonable_encoder`, and then passed to the `JSONResponse` class, which serializes it to bytes using **Python's standard JSON library**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/custom-response/]

This is an important distinction from the default behavior (without an explicit `response_class`):

> "If you declare a `response_class` with a JSON media type (`application/json`), like is the case with the `JSONResponse`, the data you return will be automatically converted (and filtered) with any Pydantic `response_model` that you declared in the *path operation decorator*. But the data won't be serialized to JSON bytes with Pydantic, instead it will be converted with the `jsonable_encoder` and then passed to the `JSONResponse` class, which will serialize it to bytes using the standard JSON library in Python." [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/custom-response/]

---

## Contrast: Default Behavior (No Explicit `response_class`)

For comparison, when you declare **only** a `response_model` or return type (without specifying a `response_class`):

- FastAPI uses **Pydantic directly** (on the Rust side) to serialize the data to JSON bytes. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/response-directly/]
- FastAPI does **not** use `jsonable_encoder` or the `JSONResponse` class. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/response-directly/]
- Instead, it returns a `Response` with the `application/json` media type directly from the Pydantic-generated JSON bytes, which is **faster**. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/response-directly/]

---

## Summary Table

| Scenario | Filtering via `response_model`? | Serialization Method |
|---|---|---|
| `response_model` only (default) | ✅ Yes | Pydantic (Rust) → fast |
| `response_class` with JSON media type + `response_model` | ✅ Yes | `jsonable_encoder` → `JSONResponse` → Python stdlib JSON |

So in short: **the response model still filters and converts the data**, but the final JSON serialization is handled by `jsonable_encoder` + Python's standard JSON library (via `JSONResponse`), rather than directly by Pydantic — which is slightly less performant. [https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/custom-response/]
